evidence.quote: The stolen RSR has been sold, Reserve’s contracts were not affected, and RSR holders don’t need to do anything.

The attacker took 3.38B RSR from Binance. Between 8:53 and 9:08 PM ET on Oct 29, they swapped all of it on Uniswap v3 for 1,856 ETH ($4.1M). As far as we can see onchain, they no longer hold any RSR, though it remains possible that the onchain swaps included wash trades with obscured attacker-funded wallets. See: https://t.co/41KjOmdoVh
Before the sale, we pulled Reserve treasury-provided onchain liquidity so it couldn’t serve as the attacker’s exit. It appears that arbitrage bots and other traders bought the RSR instead.

RSR is immutable with no admin keys, so no one, including us, can freeze it. The RSR token and Reserve protocol contracts were not affected. Since the attacker apparently no longer holds RSR, we believe it can’t be used in bulk against Reserve DTF governance.

items.author: Tristan0x
items.new_information: 端到端232ms，交易逻辑可忽略，下单190ms是主瓶颈

evidence.quote: The bot now timestamps every step from a Binance price update to our new order resting on Bullet, and exports it all to Grafana. Averaged over 5 minutes:
2. Binance to us: 41.6ms
4. Our code deciding (tick-to-trade): 0.0057ms
5. Order to live on Bullet: 190ms
End-to-end: 232ms

Speeding up one part only helps as much as that part's share of the total. Our trading logic is 0.002% of the trip. Make it 99% faster and the whole trip gets about 0.002% faster. Days of work, basically nothing to show for it.
• Binance to us (41.6ms) is distance. Part 4 moves the bot next to the exchange. Hint hint, colocation.
• Order to live (190ms) is our naive executor. It cancels the old order, waits for Bullet to confirm, then places the new one, and waits on every request. Part 6 fixes that.

To be clear, this strat rn has no edge. The defaults are deliberately wide and tiny, and it's slow: every order is synchronously waited on before the next event is read. It also measures no latency numbers yet.

Retail customer assets are generally accounted for in an omnibus account with all other retail customer assets, and customers have a claim on a pro rata share.

PayPal's card and user data survived 2014 because domain admin on the corp network couldn't unlock it quickly enough, and our alerting caught the unusual activity on the network. That's the model. Approval policy no laptop or vendor login can reach. Velocity and anomaly limits enforced outside the system that sends. Dynamic caps on what any one wallet,
account or service can move per hour. All of it in real time.

About $3B of what left Binance has been frozen, almost all of it stablecoins. The $1.4B in bitcoin is sitting in 19 wallets and nobody can touch it. I don't think that's the problem. server. Attackers can’t get the keys from the hardware, but they can ask the hardware to sign things, such as a transaction paying the attacker all of the money. evidence.quote: Later today, we are officially ending all remaining support for the Iron Fish network.

A few days ago, we observed abnormal activity involving wIRON and the ChainPort bridge. After working with ChainPort and reviewing their logs, we discovered that the cause was an inflation bug in the Iron Fish blockchain itself.

We traced the bug to a commit from early 2019 in the Merkle tree implementation. The developer at the time implemented a standard Merkle tree. However, because of nuances in how a note’s nullifier is calculated (the mechanism that lets a normal user spend their funds), the attacker was able to spend the same note more than once.
For closure, we’ve committed the patch for the exploit, with a detailed postmortem included in the PR, before shutting down and archiving the ironfish repo.
